newsitem.title: USA: Fed expected to buy bills/coupons, timing unclear.
newsitem.headline: Fed expected to buy bills/coupons, timing unclear.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is expected to add permanent reserves to the banking system sometime in the next month, U.S. Treasury market analysts said, although the timing is unclear.
Also tough to predict is whether the New York Fed's open market desk will buy bills or coupons, analysts said.

"It could come today," said Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities LLC on Wednesday. "But, they may wait until after the (Easter) holiday...It's safe to say that they could do it anytime between now until April 9."
Bostjancic projects a $10 billion add need for the maintenance period that begins on Thursday and said the Fed will most likely buy bills when it does add permanent reserves.
In February and early March, the Fed bought coupons five times over a two-week stretch totalling about $6 billion.

The the open market desk has changed the way it operates over the past few years, making it more difficult for the market to figure out the timing and maturuties involved in the Fed's next move to add permamnent reserves, analysts said.
Often in recent months, analysts have been wrong in predicting the Fed's day-to-day operations as well as its recent coupon passes. Most blamed the Fed for miscalculating reserve needs.

"You can't use historical norms anymore," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "I don't know if past purchases can be used as a guide. We have to rely more on (current) operating factor forecasts."
Flanagan recalled that in 1996, the Fed drained reserves via matched sales for much of January and February, and bought coupons on April 10 and 11.
"So, you can see, based on one, 52-week period things have changed a little bit," he said.
Flanagan said that while an outright purchase of either bills or coupons is possible the next week, it probably won't happen until after April 15.
The Fed has "to see how tax payments are coming in," he said.
Analysts said Treasury balances are skewed this time of year due to tax refunds and payments.
"There is too much risk that the money add need goes up and then comes down; there's a lot of variability," said Marc Wanshel, economist at J.P. Morgan & Co.
"I don't see the add need so unmanageable that they inject permanent reserves" until after April 15, Wanshel said. Until then, "they will want to deal with it with day-to-day operations."
